pointers.sentence: In the summer of 2005 World Online decided to release it as open source, as Django (`docs/faq/general.txt`).
The name is that of Django Reinhardt, a jazz manouche guitarist of the 1930s to the early 1950s, and it is said JANG-oh, the D silent (`docs/faq/general.txt`).

Django is distributed under the three-clause BSD licence, which grants broad permission to modify and redistribute it (`docs/faq/general.txt`); its file LICENSE names the Django Software Foundation and the individual contributors as the holders of the copyright (`django:LICENSE`).

Django is distributed under the three-clause BSD licence, which grants broad permission to modify and redistribute it (`docs/faq/general.txt`); its file LICENSE names the Django Software Foundation and the individual contributors as the holders of the copyright (`django:LICENSE`).
Python's licence stands beside it, because Django includes code from Python's standard library (`django:LICENSE.python`).

The foundation appears in the project's workings at fixed points; among them, it can fund the posts of the Django Fellows, and its board runs the elections of the steering council and ratifies their results (`docs/internals/organization.txt`).
DEP 1, which set up the process in 2014, was written by Adrian Holovaty and Jacob Kaplan-Moss and is, by its own account, a near-copy of Python's PEP process (`deps:final/0001-dep-process.rst`).

Django's documentation and DEP 19 both define a **major change** as one large enough to need a DEP, and a **minor change** as one that is not (`docs/internals/organization.txt`, `deps:accepted/0019-technical-governance-6x.rst`).

A new feature is first proposed among the project's new-feature ideas on GitHub, which the steering council reviews (`docs/internals/contributing/bugs-and-features.txt`).

Anyone may open a ticket, triage one, write a fix or review a pull request; merging, releasing and deciding belong to roles, whose present holders the project's [teams page](https://www.djangoproject.com/foundation/teams/) lists (`docs/internals/contributing/triaging-tickets.txt`, `docs/internals/organization.txt`):

**The steering council**, five members, oversees development and the release process, selects the mergers and the releasers, may make a binding decision on any question of a technical change to Django, and accepts or rejects the proposals for major changes (`deps:final/0001-dep-process.rst`).

**The security team** receives the reports of vulnerabilities (`docs/internals/security.txt`), and may ask for a security release at a time of its choosing (`deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`, `deps:accepted/0019-technical-governance-6x.rst`).

**The triage and review team** are regular contributors with extra permissions on GitHub for processing pull requests (`deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`).

**The Django Fellows** are paid by the foundation for work that includes triaging issues, reviewing and merging pull requests and managing releases (`deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`); a merger or a releaser need not be a Fellow (`docs/internals/organization.txt`).

DEP 10, written that year by James Bennett, dissolved the team of committers: push access was left to the mergers, the first of them the Fellows of the day, and uploads to the releasers; "Django Core Developer" became an honorary title; and the technical board was given the powers to decide, to veto, and to choose the mergers and the releasers (`deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`).

DEP 12, written in 2022 by Andrew Godwin, renamed the board the steering council, widened who could stand for it, and added a way to force a new election when the council neglects its duties, because recent boards acted mostly as a last hurdle for proposals and appointments and the latest election had found five candidates for five seats (`deps:final/0012-steering-council.rst`).

Django's documentation describes an organization drawn from DEP 10 and DEP 12, and those two DEPs, each of which now calls itself a historical document, send their reader to it for how the council works (`docs/internals/organization.txt`, `deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`, `deps:final/0012-steering-council.rst`).

One difference is in the mergers' rule in the list of roles: the documentation also lets a member of the steering council approve a merger's own change, and DEP 19 does not (`deps:accepted/0019-technical-governance-6x.rst`).

A change to the governance is adopted only once the foundation's board votes for it, and neither the documentation nor the DEPs record that vote for DEP 19 (`deps:final/0010-new-governance.rst`); nor does DEP 19's state tell, since a DEP for such a change is "accepted" both before that vote and after, until its implementation is complete (`deps:final/0001-dep-process.rst`).

Django's stability promise is that code written against one release keeps working with later ones, apart from minor changes their release notes list as backwards incompatible (`docs/misc/api-stability.txt`).

The security policy draws the same line from the other side: a vulnerability that depends on calling Django's private, undocumented functions in an unsafe way is not a valid report (`docs/internals/security.txt`).

`Model._meta`, the `Options` each model class carries, begins with an underscore and is documented all the same, as the Model `_meta` API (`django/db/models/options.py:Options`, `docs/ref/models/meta.txt`).

The other way round, `QuerySet.query` has no underscore and the documentation calls it an opaque object outside the public API (`docs/ref/models/querysets.txt`); and of the app registry's methods only those the documentation lists are public, which leaves out `Apps.populate`, the method `django.setup` calls (`docs/ref/applications.txt`).

Since 1.8, Django has made a feature release about every eight months, every third one a **long-term support release** that receives security and data-loss fixes for at least three years, with patch releases between (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`, `deps:final/0004-release-schedule.rst`, `docs/releases/1.8.txt`).

Under DEP 20, accepted, the release after 6.2 is Django 2028.0, not 7.0, the first of one feature release a year, each supported for three years (`deps:accepted/0020-annual-release-cycle.rst`); the releases and their dates are in [What changed](../changes.md#the-releases).

On the day, the patches are applied to main, to the two newest release series and to the long-term support releases still supported, new releases are uploaded, and a post on the project's blog describes the issue; an issue that affects only main is fixed in public (`docs/internals/security.txt`).
